article.overview: Laser-induced plasma spectroscopy, usually called laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), identifies the chemical elements in a rock or soil sample by firing a short, intense laser pulse at a small spot and analysing the light emitted by the resulting plasma. In lunar exploration, a LIBS instrument would provide rapid in-situ elemental analysis of surface material near a lander or rover. The best-documented flight experience comes from Mars rover instruments. On the Moon, the only surface operation identified in the sources reviewed for this article is the LIBS instrument carried by India's Chandrayaan-3 Pragyan rover, which landed in the lunar south polar region in August 2023; its results were reported as preliminary [3][4]. Several other lunar LIBS concepts are at study or prototype stage [7].
article.description:
A LIBS instrument has two main parts: a pulsed laser focused onto the target, and an optical system that collects the light emitted by the plasma and passes it to one or more spectrometers. Each laser pulse vaporises and ionises a very small amount of material, creating a hot, short-lived plasma. As the plasma cools, atoms and ions emit light at characteristic wavelengths. The resulting spectrum acts as a chemical fingerprint, and analysis of its emission lines identifies the elements present in the target [1][2].

The attraction of LIBS for planetary exploration is that it needs little or no sample preparation, can record several elements from a single laser shot and can operate at a distance. Mars instruments such as ChemCam are designed for stand-off analysis [1][2]. ISRO describes the Pragyan LIBS as determining the chemical and mineralogical composition of the surface [3]. The instruments differ in laser design, working distance, spectral coverage and mass, so no single description covers every LIBS payload.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The primary purpose of a lunar LIBS instrument is in-situ elemental analysis of regolith and rock at the landing site. Elemental abundances help scientists interpret the origin of surface materials and the processes that have shaped them, although any such interpretation depends on calibrated, published measurements. For the lunar south polar region, one application of particular interest is the detection of sulphur and other elements that bear on the region's surface chemistry. ISRO said the Chandrayaan-3 LIBS detection of sulphur near the south pole confirmed its presence unequivocally [4]. Target elements listed before landing were magnesium, aluminium, silicon, potassium, calcium, titanium and iron [3]. Post-landing reporting listed aluminium, sulphur, calcium, iron, chromium, titanium, manganese, silicon and oxygen, with hydrogen still under investigation [4]. These results are preliminary and should not be treated as peer-reviewed quantitative compositions.
article.operating_principle:
A LIBS measurement begins when a pulsed laser is focused onto a surface. The pulse energy is concentrated into a spot small enough to create a plasma from a tiny volume of material. In the ChemCam design described in the mission literature, the laser operates at 1067 nm, an infrared wavelength invisible to the eye, and the plasma light is collected and carried by optical fibre to spectrometers [1][2]. The spectrometers separate the light by wavelength, and analysis software compares the emission lines with reference data and calibration standards to estimate elemental composition. Working distance affects the laser spot size, the collection of plasma light and the energy delivered to the target, which is why stand-off performance is a central design parameter [2]. The MicroLIBS abstract describes an adjustable working distance of 20 to 50 cm and an ablated spot of 50 to 100 micrometres [7].

The lunar surface has no appreciable atmosphere, whereas ChemCam and other Mars instruments operate through the Martian atmosphere. This is a difference in the physical environment of the plasma, but the sources reviewed here do not quantify its effect on the measurements. Mars-derived calibration should therefore not be assumed to transfer unchanged to lunar conditions.
article.scientific_importance: The Moon's surface composition has been mapped remotely, but orbital spectrometers measure radiation that is indirect and affected by surface maturity, grain size and space weathering. An in-situ LIBS measurement can provide direct elemental information from a specific spot at a known location. Mars LIBS instruments have demonstrated the technique's value for rock and soil analysis over long operating periods [1][2][10]. If the Chandrayaan-3 results are confirmed in peer-reviewed analysis, they would be significant as in-situ LIBS measurements near the lunar south pole [3][4]. The scientific importance of a lunar LIBS instrument therefore lies both in its geological capability and in its ability to ground-truth orbital data and inform future polar exploration.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a LIBS payload. Laser energy and wavelength, working distance, spectrometer design, detectors, thermal control, mass and power depend on the mission architecture. The examples below describe specific instruments or concepts and must not be generalised. LIBS-specific mass, power and dimensions for the Chandrayaan-3 instrument are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed, so rover-level figures are shown separately.

examples.name: Chandrayaan-2 Pragyan rover LIBS (planned, not operated)
examples.type: Planned lunar surface instrument; never operated on the Moon
examples.status: Lost with the lander in September 2019; the rover was never deployed
examples.description: A LIBS instrument was part of the planned payload of the Chandrayaan-2 Pragyan rover, indicated by a reference title in the rover's Wikipedia article [6]. The lander crashed on 6 September 2019 and the rover was never deployed, so this example has no lunar operating record. The rover's mass of about 27 kg is a rover-level figure from the same source [6]. No LIBS-specific specification was found in the sources reviewed for this article.

examples.name: Chandrayaan-3 Pragyan rover LIBS
examples.type: Flown and operated lunar surface instrument
examples.status: Operated on the lunar surface after landing in the south polar region on 23 August 2023; results reported as preliminary
examples.description:
The Chandrayaan-3 Pragyan rover carried a LIBS instrument developed by ISRO's Laboratory for Electro-Optics Systems (LEOS) in Bengaluru [4]. The lander and rover made a soft landing in the lunar south polar region on 23 August 2023 [3]. The mission goal was to operate the rover for about one lunar day, or roughly 14 Earth days, and the lander and rover were not designed to survive the lunar night [3]. Reported rover figures include a mass of 26 kg and generation of about 50 W [5]; these are rover values and are not LIBS-specific. The LIBS elemental results were reported as preliminary [4].

examples.name: ChemCam (Mars Science Laboratory, Curiosity rover)
examples.type: Flown Mars LIBS instrument; not a lunar instrument; flight-heritage analogue
examples.status: Operating on Mars since the Curiosity mission began; no lunar operation
examples.description: ChemCam is a Mars LIBS instrument on NASA's Curiosity rover, described as the first LIBS instrument on Mars [1]. Its laser operates at 1067 nm [1]. The working distance for analysis is commonly given as 1.3 to 7 m [2]; other summaries give 1.5 to 7 m or 1 to 9 m, so the published range is not fully resolved. Reported laser pulses are under 5 ns with more than 10 mJ per pulse [9], and an ISAE poster gives 14 mJ on target with a spot of about 350 micrometres [8]. The repetition rate is 1 to 10 Hz with a nominal 3 Hz [9]. The spectral coverage of 240 to 800 nm is given in the ISAE poster [8] but has not been checked against a primary instrument paper.
examples.stand_off_distance_m: 1.3 to 7 (most commonly cited; other summaries differ)
examples.pulse_energy_mj: more than 10 per pulse (reported); 14 on target (ISAE poster)
examples.spectral_range_nm: 240 to 800 (ISAE poster; not verified against a primary instrument paper)

examples.name: SuperCam (Mars 2020, Perseverance rover)
examples.type: Flown Mars instrument that includes a LIBS subsystem; not a lunar instrument
examples.status: Operating on Mars since the rover's arrival in February 2021
examples.description: SuperCam on NASA's Perseverance rover includes a LIBS subsystem and has been used on Mars since the rover's arrival in February 2021 [10]. This article does not provide quantitative specifications for the SuperCam LIBS subsystem because the primary specification sources were not verified in this run.

examples.name: MicroLIBS (CNES and partner concept and prototype)
examples.type: Prototype and concept for a lightweight LIBS micro-mapper; not flown
examples.status: Prototype being assembled at CNES according to the 2025 abstract; target TRL close to 6 with tests in early 2026
examples.description: MicroLIBS is a lightweight LIBS concept and prototype developed by a team from IRAP (Toulouse), CNES, LANL, Purdue, the University of Iowa and DLR [7]. The abstract gives a mass limit of 1.5 kg for the Mars configuration, a working distance of 20 to 50 cm, an ablated spot of 50 to 100 micrometres and a laser repetition rate of up to 10 Hz [7]. The prototype was being assembled at CNES, and the team stated a target of raising TRL close to 6 with dedicated tests in early 2026 [7]. The abstract says the technology can be adapted to the Moon, icy moons and small bodies [7]; this is a stated adaptation possibility, not a lunar mission commitment. The concept has not flown.
examples.mass_note: Maximum allowance for the Mars configuration, from the abstract

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not publicly specified for the Chandrayaan-3 LIBS. Dimensions for ChemCam, SuperCam and MicroLIBS were not verified in this run, except that MicroLIBS is described as a lightweight micro-mapper with an adjustable 20 to 50 cm working distance [7]. Dimensions depend on the laser, optics, spectrometer and thermal design and must be tied to a named instrument.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Only a limit is published for MicroLIBS in its Mars configuration (maximum 1.5 kg) [7]. The Chandrayaan-3 rover mass of 26 kg [5] and the Chandrayaan-2 rover mass of 27 kg [6] are rover-level figures, not LIBS masses. The LIBS mass for the Chandrayaan-3 instrument is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified for the Chandrayaan-3 LIBS. A rover-level figure of about 50 W is reported for the Chandrayaan-3 rover [5]; this includes the rover and is not a LIBS power budget.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar LIBS payload would face vacuum, extreme surface temperature variation, lunar dust, radiation and the mechanical loads of landing. Its optics must stay aligned and clean, since dust on laser or collection optics could degrade measurements. The instrument also needs a defined working distance or placement relative to the target. The Chandrayaan-3 rover was not designed to survive the lunar night [3], which constrains surface LIBS operations. Mars-derived calibration and plasma interpretation must be adapted for vacuum and lunar regolith surfaces, and the sources reviewed do not quantify this for any lunar LIBS instrument.
article.limitations: LIBS measures emission from a very small, heated volume of material. Results depend on calibration and matrix effects, so quantitative composition requires reference standards and careful analysis. Light elements and hydrogen can be difficult to quantify; for Chandrayaan-3, ISRO's hydrogen determination was still under investigation [4]. Working distance is a design trade-off: the ChemCam design spans a stand-off range [2], while MicroLIBS is designed for placement at 20 to 50 cm [7]. A single measurement spot may not represent a wider area. The Chandrayaan-3 results are preliminary and were reported through agency and science-news coverage rather than a peer-reviewed paper located during this research.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A LIBS payload would reach the surface as an instrument on a lander or rover. In the Chandrayaan-3 mission, the LIBS was part of the rover payload, which operated on the surface after landing [3][4]. The sources reviewed do not describe the rover's deployment or interface mechanisms in detail, so no lander-specific interface is described in this article.
transportation_process: Integrate the LIBS on Earth into the rover or lander payload, verifying laser safety, thermal provisions and optical alignment.
Launch on a launch vehicle and transfer towards the Moon.
Land and deliver the rover or surface payload to the lunar surface.
Deploy the rover or instrument, confirm the working distance to the target, and connect power, thermal and data interfaces.
Operate within the surface mission window, respecting thermal and power limits, including any lunar-night constraint.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: For the Chandrayaan-3 example, the LIBS was a rover-associated instrument, and the sources do not describe a separate deployment mechanism for it. For a close-range concept such as MicroLIBS, a working distance of 20 to 50 cm implies a defined placement relative to the target, which may require a pointing or arm-based mechanism. The MicroLIBS abstract does not describe a flight deployment method for the Moon [7].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Chandrayaan-3 Pragyan operated a LIBS on the lunar surface in 2023 [3][4]. Chandrayaan-2 Pragyan was planned to carry a LIBS but was lost with its lander [6]. Mars LIBS instruments such as ChemCam and SuperCam operated from rovers [1][10].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander or rover compatibility is asserted. A LIBS instrument's suitability for a particular lunar lander would depend on its mass, mounting, pointing or arm interface, power, thermal control and data routing. Such a comparison requires verified spacecraft interface data, which were not reviewed for this article.

article.historical_significance: LIBS has substantial Mars heritage. ChemCam on Curiosity is described as the first LIBS instrument on Mars [1]. The Chandrayaan-2 mission planned a LIBS-equipped rover, which was lost when the lander crashed in September 2019 [6]. The Chandrayaan-3 Pragyan rover then carried a LIBS to the lunar south polar region in 2023 [3][4]. Based on the sources reviewed, this is the most significant lunar LIBS operation identified in this research, although its results are preliminary. Search-level summaries also mention MarSCoDe on China's Zhurong rover as a Mars LIBS instrument; this was not verified against a primary source and is noted only as an unverified lead. Lunar LIBS concepts, including MicroLIBS [7], indicate continuing interest in the technique.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name 'laser-induced plasma spectrometer' describes a measurement technique and a class of instruments rather than one standard design. The ChemCam, SuperCam, Chandrayaan-3 and MicroLIBS examples differ substantially, and their values must not be combined. Key evidence gaps: (1) LIBS-specific mass, power, dimensions, laser and spectrometer specifications for the Chandrayaan-3 instrument are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed; (2) the Chandrayaan-3 element detections are preliminary post-landing reports, and the target and measured element lists differ between sources; (3) ChemCam working-distance and spectral-range figures conflict between sources; (4) the full texts of the Wiens et al. and Maurice et al. 2012 papers (Springer) and of a DLR MicroLIBS paper could not be accessed, so instrument-level claims rely on abstracts or summaries; (5) the Chandrayaan-2 LIBS is documented only by a reference title; (6) the MicroLIBS status after its early-2026 test target is unknown.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue ID 075, name 'Laser-induced plasma spectrometer' and category 3 'Mineralogical and chemical analysis' verified against lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md. The catalogue was not edited.

Full texts of Wiens et al. 2012 and Maurice et al. 2012 (Springer) could not be accessed (redirect to login). Their DOIs are cited, but instrument-level statements from them rest on search-level abstracts and summaries.
The DLR applsci 14 02467 PDF returned an access-denied page and is not used as a source.

ChemCam working distance (1.3 to 7 m commonly; 1.5 to 7 m and 1 to 9 m in other summaries), pulse energy (more than 10 mJ vs 14 mJ on target), and spectral range (240 to 800 nm from one poster) are inconsistent or unverified across sources.

Chandrayaan-3 LIBS element results are preliminary post-landing reports, relayed through ISRO-linked coverage and Spectroscopy Online (2023). No peer-reviewed paper was located. Hydrogen was still under investigation.

No LIBS-specific mass, power, dimensions, laser or spectrometer specifications are publicly specified for Chandrayaan-3 in the sources reviewed. The rover mass (26 kg in the Commons caption, 27 kg for the Chandrayaan-2 rover on Wikipedia) and rover power (about 50 W) are separate rover-level figures and are not compared.
Chandrayaan-2 LIBS is supported only by a reference title in the Wikipedia article; no operational or specification detail was verified.

Image: the direct URL was taken from the Wikimedia Commons file page. The asset was not downloaded or checked for full resolution. The licence is GODL-India and the Commons page says it had not been reviewed by an administrator. The image shows the rover, not the LIBS subsystem, and its type (photograph or rendering) is not confirmed. Source is not an official agency image asset.
No direct image URLs were verified for ChemCam, SuperCam or MicroLIBS, so those examples carry no images rather than unverified ones.
MicroLIBS: the TRL and test targets are stated goals from the 2025 abstract; the status after early 2026 is not verified.
Lunar LIBS work from a 2007 Chinese feasibility study and the MarSCoDe (Zhurong) LIBS data were seen only in search summaries and are not used as article claims.

The MSL ChemCam reference (pulse energy and repetition rate) is cited at the site root after removing the original query string; the specific page was seen only in search summaries and was not opened.
No lander or rover compatibility is asserted, and no landing-site or location recommendation is included, per the user's deferral.
